arXiv:2510.15056v1 [cs.LG] 16 Oct 2025

Learn to Change the World: Multi-level Reinforcement Learning with Model-Changing Actions

Ziqing Lu Affiliation: University of Iowa Email: ziqlu@uiowa.edu    Babak Hassibi Affiliation: California Institude of Technology Email: hassibi@systems.caltech.edu    Lifeng Lai Affiliation: University of California, Davis Email: lflai@ucdavis.edu    Weiyu Xu Affiliation: University of Iowa Email: weiyu-xu@uiowa.edu
Abstract

Reinforcement learning usually assumes a given or sometimes even fixed environment in which an agent seeks an optimal policy to maximize its long-term discounted reward. In contrast, we consider agents that are not limited to passive adaptations: they instead have model-changing actions that actively modify the RL model of world dynamics itself. Reconfiguring the underlying transition processes can potentially increase the agents’ rewards. Motivated by this setting, we introduce the multi-layer configurable time-varying Markov decision process (MCTVMDP). In an MCTVMDP, the lower-level MDP has a non-stationary transition function that is configurable through upper-level model-changing actions. The agent’s objective consists of two parts: Optimize the configuration policies in the upper-level MDP and optimize the primitive action policies in the lower-level MDP to jointly improve its expected long-term reward.

   

Keywords reinforcement learning, optimization, robust learning

1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning, which is based on the mathematical model Markov decision process (MDP), has been widely applied in many real-world sequential decision problems, such as in RLHF [1], in financial decisions [2], and in robotic control algorithms [3], etc. There are sufficient works in finding optimal policies in a fixed environment, through both model-based approaches [4] such as planning on estimated models, and model-free approaches such as variants of Q-learning [5] and variants of policy gradient methods [6]. However, in many applications, an MDP environment can be changed on purpose in order to increase the obtainable rewards.

In this paper, we consider a new framework of MDP-based reinforcement learning (RL). In this new type of RL framework, an agent have actions which it can execute to change the involved MDP model itself. These changes include, but are not limited to, changing its transition kernels, rewards, and even the set of allowable later actions. Traditionally, in the RL MDP models, state transitions after taking actions still follow the same underlying statistical model, and these actions can only potentially change the states the agents are in. In other words, a traditional RL behaves within a pre-specified statistical model, and this statistical model stays unchanged no matter what actions are taken. In contrast, the new RL framework proposed in this paper have the potential and mechanism of breaking out of the current model, through actions that change or improve the underlying MDP. For example, consider an RL agent with actions that can change the transition kernels of the underlying MDP. After model-changing actions are taken at certain time steps of the MDP, the transition kernel in the following time steps will be changed but remains constant until further model-changing actions are taken.

As special cases of the proposed RL mechanism with model-changing actions, we consider configurable RL for time-varying environments and multi-level (including bi-level) environment-changing RLs. In the configurable RL for a time-varying environment, after a certain number of time steps, the transition kernel will be changed to a different transition kernel by nature. The agent then takes action at that time step that can change or improve the transition kernel. In the bi-level RL scheme, the lower-level RL is responsible for finding the optimal policy given a certain RL configuration, while the upper-level MDP is responsible for finding the optimal policy for configuring the lower-level MDP. The lower-level MDP’s quantities, which the upper-level MDP can configure, thus become the states of the upper-level MDP. For example, if the upper-level MDP is exploring actions configuring the lower-level MDP’s transition kernel, the lower level’s transition kernel becomes the state of the upper-level MDP. This is interesting since within a single MDP model, the states and the transition kernel between them are completely different subjects or concepts; however, in the unique multi-level MDP setting considered in this paper, the lower-level transition kernel can become the state of the upper MDP. To the best of our knowledge, such formulations where the transition kernels become upper-level MDP’s states are rare or unseen before in the literature.

Let us consider an example of a 3-level MDP framework with model-changing actions. The highest level, namely the 3rd level, of this framework is an MDP which represents the evolution of the politics and legislation of a country: this MDP’s states are the evolving approved guidelines (fiscal policies) for this country’s central bank, and the actions are the efforts of legislation. Note that legislative efforts can potentially result in random fiscal policies that depend on political unexpected political compromises and random political events. The 2nd-level MDP represents the dynamics of the central bank setting up and exploring monetary policies: the states of this 2nd-level MDP are the monetary policies, and the transition kernel between the monetary policies is affected by the fiscal policies set by the 3rd-level MDP. The actions on this 2nd level are monetary policy explorations, such as motions to change the Federal Reserve interest rates. These actions may result in random-sized interest rate changes due to monetary policy voting results and random foreign countries’ economic environments. The 1st-level MDP represents the society’s economic activities: this lower-level MDP’s states are the situations of the society’s productions and consumptions of goods and services, and the transition kernel between the states is dictated or configured by the monetary policies adopted in the 2nd-level MDP.

Consider another example of a robot trying to cross a fast-flowing river. Without changing the environment, the robot performs RL on non-model-changing maneuvers e.g., moving left, right, backward, forward, upward, or downward) to adapt to the river flow, but may still be swept away with a high probability if the current is too strong. In our model-changing RL setting, the robot can instead modify the environment of this river, for example, by placing stepping stones in the river. This naturally leads to a bi-level MDP with model-changing actions. The state in the upper-level MDP is the configuration of the river environment, dictating the transition kernel for the lower MDP for the robot’s non-model-changing maneuvers. The upper-level MDP’s actions are the robot’s actions, which change the configuration of the river environment. We note that the robot’s actions of putting stepping stones into the river can lead to transitions to random configurations of the river environment, because it is random whether a deployed stone is washed away or stays still in place under the river current. The lower-level actions are the robot’s non-model-changing maneuvers under a given river environment. The states affected by the lower-level actions are the locations of the robot in the river.

Motivated by these examples, this paper makes the following contributions: 1) We formulated the problem of RL with model-changing actions; and we proposed two special models for RL with model-changing actions: multi-level configurable MDPs and time-varying configurable MDP; 2) We proposed algorithms including convex optimization formulations and multi-level value iterations for solving multi-level configurable RL problems; 3) We proved theoretical performance guarantees for the proposed algorithms; 4) We provided numerical results showing the effectiveness of configuring or improving favorable RL environment through learning.

Related works: The literature most closely related to our work is configurable MDP (CMDP) [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14], where the agent can configure some environmental parameters to improve the performance of a learning agent. Within the series of works in configurable MDP, [11] assumes that a “better” world configuration corresponds to a transition probability matrix whose corresponding optimal policy yields a larger total discounted reward. They formulate the problem of reasoning over “good” world configurations as a non-convex constrained optimization problem, where the agent explicitly balances the benefits of changing the world against the costs incurred by such modifications. Unlike our approach, their formulation does not employ upper-level MDP abstractions/learning to model/improve configuration actions, but relies on direct gradient-based optimization. In addition, our paper deals with time-varying non-stationary lower-level MDPs.

[10] addresses how to optimize configurations for a contextual MDP where some parameters are configurable while others are stochastic. Their bi-level gradient-based formulation (BO-MDP) can be viewed as a Stackelberg game where the leader and a random context beyond the leader’s control together configure an MDP, while (potentially many) followers optimize their strategies given the setting. [9] focuses on regulating the agent’s interaction with the environment by redesigning the reward or transition kernel parameters. They formulate this problem as a bi-level program, in which the upper-level designer regulates the lower-level MDP, aiming to induce desired policies in the agent and achieve system-level objectives. In contrast with these works, our work places the configuration process under the control of the RL agent itself, which adjusts/configures the lower-level kernels with the goal of maximizing its own reward. In our work, the RL model has built-in actions that can change the model itself, which is not the case in previous works. Moreover, in our setting, upper-level configurations are explicitly modeled as an MDP, which is unlike the one-time configuration in previous works. [8] analyzes the complexity of solving CMDPs, demonstrates several parameterizations of CMDPs, and derives a gradient-based solution approach. Their approach, particularly in the continuous configuration setting, is related to our linear approximation method for solving the special case of TVCMDPs. However, our primary contribution lies in the study of multi-layer configurable MDPs. which differs fundamentally from the continuous framework in [8]. Our work also covers time-varying transition kernels, which were not investigated by these previous works. A unique characteristic of our framework is that the transition kernels of lower-level MDPs actually become the states of an upper-level MDP.

Our work is different from hierarchical RL/MDP [15] because in our multilayer model, the upper-level MDP is built upon choosing (configuring) a better transition kernel, while hierarchical MDP deals with decomposing long-horizon tasks into simpler subtasks or learning hierarchical policies. For other literature on non-stationary environments, such as semi-MDP [16], Meta-RL [17] and Bayesian MDPs [18], the key distinction from our formulation lies in the design-driven “configuration” nature of configurable MDPs: the agent is allowed to modify the environment itself to improve its potential returns. In semi-MDPs, the agent can only temporally extend actions, but the environment remains fixed. In contrast, in a configurable MDP the agent can choose both the environment configuration and an associated policy. Meta-RL aims to train the agent across a distribution of tasks to enable rapid adaptation to unseen tasks, while the configurable MDP assumes a known set of configurations, and the agent’s goal is to pick the best environment and policy.

2 Problem formulation

General ideas of a framework with model-changing actions: We consider an “MDP” ℳC={𝒮,𝒜,P,T,r,γ}\mathcal{M}_{C}=\{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,T,r,\gamma\} having actions which can change its transition kernel. In ℳC\mathcal{M}_{C}, 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the state space with |𝒮|=n|\mathcal{S}|=n, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the action space, the transition kernel P:𝒮×𝒜×𝒮→[0,1]P:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{S}\rightarrow[0,1] is subject to change or configuration and may be time-varying. rr is the reward function and γ\gamma is the discounting factor. Different from a regular MDP, at certain time steps, the agent may adopt model-changing actions which can change the MDP to have a new (maybe random) transition kernel, and this new transition kernel will remain fixed until another new model-changing action adopted in the future changes the transition kernel again.

Because the transition kernels can change over time due to model-changing actions, most traditional theories for MDP do not apply. We consider the following special cases called multi-level configurable MDP where the time steps are divided into episodes, and the model-changing actions are only taken at the beginning of each episode. The model-changing actions are actions of upper-level MDPs which dictate or change the transition kernels of lower-level MDPs. We focus on bi-level configurable MDPs, which can be extended to multi-level MDP in a similar way.

Bi-level configurable MDP: We build a bi-level configurable MDP that separates model-changing actions (configuration operations) from primitive actions, using an episodic-style hierarchical structure. For the upper-level model, the agent chooses a model-changing action at the start of each episode that configures the lower-level environment by selecting a lower-level transition kernel. This configuration determines the dynamics for the entire episode. Sequential decisions on model-changing actions throughout episodes form an upper-level MDP, aiming to optimize the model-changing policy and to improve the lower-level model over time. There is a cost imposed on taking a model-changing action, which is represented as a penalty included in the upper-level reward function. For the lower-level model, within each episode, the agent interacts with a standard MDP with the current transition kernel set by the upper level. The agent normally selects primitive actions, receives rewards, and aims to optimize its policy. We use kk to denote the episode steps and use tt to denote the time steps within an episode.

Mathematically, the bi-level MDP can be formulated as: a lower-level ℳL={𝒮,𝒜,P,T,μ0,r,γ}\mathcal{M}_{L}=\{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,T,\mu_{0},r,\gamma\} and an upper-level ℳU={𝒫,ℬ,Q,K,R,λ}\mathcal{M}_{U}=\{\mathcal{P},\mathcal{B},Q,K,R,\lambda\}. In ℳL\mathcal{M}_{L}, which can be considered similar to a standard MDP, 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the state space with |𝒮|=n|\mathcal{S}|=n, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the action space, the lower-level transition kernel P:𝒮×𝒜×𝒮→[0,1]P:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{S}\rightarrow[0,1] is determined by ℳU\mathcal{M}_{U} and is subject to change. We denote the transition kernel in episode kk as PkP_{k}. TT is the number of time steps within one episode and can go large (even “infinity”, relatively speaking) when we consider an “infinite-horizon” ℳL\mathcal{M}_{L}. μ0∈ℝn\mu_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is the initial state distribution of each episode and is set to be uniform. At the beginning of each episode kk , the state distribution is reset to be μ0\mu_{0}. r:𝒮×𝒜→ℝr:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is the reward function and we denote rmax=max(s,a)∈𝒮×𝒜⁡r⁡(s,a)r_{\max}=\max_{(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}}r(s,a). γ∈[0,1)\gamma\in[0,1) is the lower-level discount factor.

We use πk:𝒮→𝒜\pi_{k}:\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\mathcal{A} to denote the primitive policy of episode kk that determines the lower-level actions of the agents. For episode kk, the lower-level state-value (namely V-value) function of the agent following the policy πk\pi_{k} is:

Vπk(s)=𝔼Pk[∑t=0∞γtr(st,at)|s0=s,at∼πk],s∈𝒮V^{\pi_{k}}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{P_{k}}[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})|s_{0}=s,a_{t}\sim\pi_{k}],s\in\mathcal{S}

and the closed-form solution of the Bellman equation for the state-value function is:

Vπk=(I−γ​Pkπk)−1​rπk,\displaystyle V^{\pi_{k}}=(I-\gamma P^{\pi_{k}}_{k})^{-1}r^{\pi_{k}}, (1)

where Vπk,Pk∈ℝnV^{\pi_{k},P_{k}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is the vectorized state-values, and Pkπk,rπkP^{\pi_{k}}_{k},r^{\pi_{k}} are in the form:

Pkπk=[−Pk(⋅|s1,πk(s1))−−Pk(⋅|s2,πk(s2))−−Pk(⋅|sn,πk(sn))−],rπk=[r⁡(s1,πk​(s1))r⁡(s2,πk​(s2))r⁡(sn,πk​(sn))].\displaystyle P^{\pi_{k}}_{k}=\begin{bmatrix}-P_{k}(\cdot|s_{1},\pi_{k}(s_{1}))-\\ -P_{k}(\cdot|s_{2},\pi_{k}(s_{2}))-\\ \vdots\\ -P_{k}(\cdot|s_{n},\pi_{k}(s_{n}))-\end{bmatrix},r^{\pi_{k}}=\begin{bmatrix}r(s_{1},\pi_{k}(s_{1}))\\ r(s_{2},\pi_{k}(s_{2}))\\ \vdots\\ r(s_{n},\pi_{k}(s_{n}))\end{bmatrix}.

We denote the lower-level initial expected return J⁡(πk,Pk)J(\pi_{k},P_{k}) of episode kk as:

J⁡(πk,Pk)=μ0T​Vπk,Pk.\displaystyle J(\pi_{k},P_{k})=\mu_{0}^{T}V^{\pi_{k},P_{k}}. (2)

In ℳU\mathcal{M}_{U}, 𝒫\mathcal{P} is the space of lower-level transition kernels and is the “state” space of ℳU\mathcal{M}_{U}. For simplicity, we assume that the upper-level state 𝒫\mathcal{P} with |𝒫|=m|\mathcal{P}|=m is discrete and finite. The upper-level state P∈𝒫P\in\mathcal{P} is also the transition kernel PP of the lower-level MDP ℳL\mathcal{M}_{L}. ℬ\mathcal{B} is the set of model-changing actions. Q:𝒫×ℬ×𝒫→[0,1]Q:\mathcal{P}\times\mathcal{B}\times\mathcal{P}\rightarrow[0,1] is the upper-level kernel that determines the transitions of upper-level states. The notation of the upper-level kernel is Q⁡(P′|P,b)Q(P^{\prime}|P,b) where P′P^{\prime} is the configured lower-level kernel, and the distribution of P′P^{\prime} depends on the current lower-level kernel PP and the model-changing action bb. KK is the total number of episodes and can go to infinity when we consider an infinite-horizon ℳU\mathcal{M}_{U}. λ∈[0,1)\lambda\in[0,1) is the upper-level discount factor. R:𝒫×ℬ→ℝR:\mathcal{P}\times\mathcal{B}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is the upper-level reward function. The reward of episode kk is defined as:

R⁡(Pk,bk)=∑Pk+1∈𝒫Q⁡(Pk+1|Pk,bk)​J​(πk+1∗,Pk+1)−C⁡(Pk,bk),\displaystyle R(P_{k},b_{k})=\sum_{P_{k+1}\in\mathcal{P}}Q(P_{k+1}|P_{k},b_{k})J(\pi^{*}_{k+1},P_{k+1})-C(P_{k},b_{k}), (3)

where πk+1∗\pi^{*}_{k+1} is the optimal primitive policy of episode k+1k+1, and C⁡(Pk,bk)C(P_{k},b_{k}) is the cost function. We denote Rmax=max(P,b)∈𝒫×ℬ⁡R⁡(P,b)R_{\max}=\max_{(P,b)\in\mathcal{P}\times\mathcal{B}}R(P,b).

We let WΘ​(P)W^{\Theta}(P) denote the higher-order state-value function if the agent follows the higher-order policy of configuration operations Θ:P→ℬ\Theta:P\rightarrow\mathcal{B}:

WΘ(P)=𝔼Q[∑k=0∞λkR(Pk,bk)|P0=P,bk∼Θ],P∈𝒫W^{\Theta}(P)=\mathbb{E}_{Q}[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\lambda^{k}R(P_{k},b_{k})|P_{0}=P,b_{k}\sim\Theta],P\in\mathcal{P}

The agent aims to find an optimal higher-order policy Θ∗\Theta^{*} such that Θ∗=arg⁡maxΘ⁡WΘ\Theta^{*}=\arg\max_{\Theta}W^{\Theta}.

Special case of bi-level configurable MDPs: Time-variant MDP and continuous configuration: We consider a special case when the upper-level state space 𝒫\mathcal{P} is continuous and agents can continuously change the lower-level environment deterministically. In this case, we only consider a one-layer MDP, in which the transition kernel is time-variant throughout episodes and configurable. Additionally, the configuration operations incur costs when the agent modifies a less favorable transition kernel to a more favorable one. We study a constrained optimization problem that seeks to maximize the agent’s discounted long-term reward asymptotically as time goes to infinity, taking into account both the time-varying world dynamics and a budget constraint on the total cost of configurations.

Mathematically, the time-variant configurable MDP (TVCMDP) can be described as the following: ℳT​V​C={𝒮,𝒜,𝒞,K,{Pk}k=1K,μ0,T,r,γ}\mathcal{M}_{TVC}=\{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{C},K,\{P_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K},\mu_{0},T,r,\gamma\}, where 𝒞\mathcal{C} is the space of configuration operations, KK is the total number of episodes, and TT is the total number of time steps within each episode. The time-varying transition kernel Pk,k∈[K]P_{k},k\in[K] is determined by nature at the beginning of each episode (for example, without maintenance, road can randomly deteriorate after a period of time). All other parameters are the same as those introduced in ℳL\mathcal{M}_{L}.

Within episode kk, the configuration operation x∈𝒞\mathrm{x}\in\mathcal{C} is represented by xk∈[−1,1]n×n\mathrm{x}_{k}\in[-1,1]^{n\times n} where xk\mathrm{x}_{k} is the amount of change the agent does to the default transition kernel PkP_{k}. To evaluate the effect of configurations 𝐱={xk}k=0K\mathbf{x}=\{\mathrm{x}_{k}\}_{k=0}^{K}, we define the sum of configured function F⁡(𝐱,𝝅)F(\mathbf{x};\bm{\pi}) with the set of configuration operations 𝐱={xk}k=0K\mathbf{x}=\{\mathrm{x}_{k}\}_{k=0}^{K} and the set of primitive policies 𝝅={πk}k=0K\bm{\pi}=\{\pi_{k}\}_{k=0}^{K} as:

F⁡(𝐱,𝝅)=∑k=0KJ⁡(πk,Pk+xk),\displaystyle F(\mathbf{x};\bm{\pi})=\sum_{k=0}^{K}J(\pi_{k},P_{k}+\mathrm{x}_{k}), (4)

where J⁡(π,P)J(\pi,P) is determined by (2). The agent in TVCMDP aims to maximize the objective function (4) by optimizing the configuration variables 𝐱\bm{\mathrm{x}}.

3 Cost-constrained optimization problem on TVCMDP

Cost constrained optimization problem: Recall that in TVCDMP, the agent wants to maximize the objective function (4) by optimizing the configuration variables xk\mathrm{x}_{k} throughout the KK episodes. The original cost-constrained objective function under the configuration budget is (5),

maxxk⁡maxπk\displaystyle\max_{\mathrm{x}_{k}}\max_{\pi_{k}}\; ∑k=0KJ⁡(πk,Pk+xk),\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{K}J(\pi_{k},P_{k}+\mathrm{x}_{k}), (5)
s.t.  ∑k=0KC⁡(xk)≤B,\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{K}C(\mathrm{x}_{k})\leq B,
∑j=1n(Pkπk+xk)i​j=1,∀i,k,\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{n}\big(P^{\pi_{k}}_{k}+\mathrm{x}_{k}\big)_{ij}=1,\quad\forall i,k,
0≤(Pkπk+xk)i​j≤1,∀i,j,k,\displaystyle 0\leq\big(P^{\pi_{k}}_{k}+\mathrm{x}_{k}\big)_{ij}\leq 1,\quad\forall i,j,k,

where BB is the configuration budget, and C⁡(xk)C(\mathrm{x}_{k}) is the cost function of changing the default transition kernel by xk\mathrm{x}_{k}. Because configuration to the environment may be a highly-costly operation, we assume that the cost grows exponentially as the amount of configuration increases, i.e., C⁡(x)=∑i​jβ⁡(eα​|(x)i,j|−1)C(\mathrm{x})=\sum_{ij}\beta(e^{\alpha|(\mathrm{x})_{i,j}|}-1), where α,β∈ℝ\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R} are non-negative constants, and α\alpha can be large. To solve this cost-constrained optimization problem, we first linearize the objective function (4). As a by-product, we also solve out the Jacobian ∇PπVπ∈ℝn×n×n\nabla_{P^{\pi}}V^{\pi}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n\times n} of VπV^{\pi} with respect to PπP^{\pi}. Please see Appendix A.

≈(I−γ​Pπ)−1​rπ−(I−γ​Pπ)−1​(−γ​x)​(I−γ​Pπ)−1​rπ\displaystyle\approx(I-\gamma P^{\pi})^{-1}r^{\pi}-(I-\gamma P^{\pi})^{-1}(-\gamma\mathrm{x})(I-\gamma P^{\pi})^{-1}r^{\pi}
=(I−γ​Pπ)−1​rπ+γ​(I−γ​Pπ)−1​x​(I−γ​Pπ)−1​rπ\displaystyle=(I-\gamma P^{\pi})^{-1}r^{\pi}+\gamma(I-\gamma P^{\pi})^{-1}\mathrm{x}(I-\gamma P^{\pi})^{-1}r^{\pi}

We let matrix M=γ​(I−γ​Pπ)−1,M∈ℝn×nM=\gamma(I-\gamma P^{\pi})^{-1},M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, and let vector N=(I−γ​Pπ)−1​rπ,N∈ℝnN=(I-\gamma P^{\pi})^{-1}r^{\pi},N\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. The above formula can be rewritten as:

Vπ​(Pπ+x)≈N+M​x​N\displaystyle V^{\pi}(P^{\pi}+\mathrm{x})\approx N+M\mathrm{x}N (6)

Convex optimization problem: We can now rewrite the original optimization problem (5) by applying the linear approximation (6). Now the Nk∈ℝnN_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and Mk∈ℝn×nM_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} are associated with episode kk. The objective function can be rewritten as maxxk⁡max⁡∑k=0Kπk⁡μ0T​Nk+μ0T​Mk​xk​Nk.\max_{\mathrm{x}_{k}}\max_{\pi_{k}}\sum_{k=0}^{K}\mu_{0}^{T}N_{k}+\mu_{0}^{T}M_{k}\mathrm{x}_{k}N_{k}. We can ignore the constant term μ0T​Nk\mu_{0}^{T}N_{k}. Since μ0T​Mk​xk​Nk\mu_{0}^{T}M_{k}\mathrm{x}_{k}N_{k} is a scalar, we have μ0T​Mk​xk​Nk=t​r​(μT​Mk​xk​Nk)\mu_{0}^{T}M_{k}\mathrm{x}_{k}N_{k}=tr(\mu^{T}M_{k}\mathrm{x}_{k}N_{k}), and t​r​(⋅)tr(\cdot) is the matrix trace function. If we let AkT=Nk​μ0T​MkA^{T}_{k}=N_{k}\mu_{0}^{T}M_{k}, this objective function is equal to ⟨Ak,xk⟩=∑i​j(Ak)i​j​(xk)i​j\langle A_{k},x_{k}\rangle=\sum_{ij}(A_{k})_{ij}(\mathrm{x}_{k})_{ij}, and Ak=MkT​μ0​NkTA_{k}=M_{k}^{T}\mu_{0}N^{T}_{k}, Ak∈ℝn×nA_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}.

We assume that the cost function is point-wise exponential and BB is the total cost budget, i.e., ∑k≤K,i,j≤n(eα​|(xk)i​j|−1)≤B\sum_{k\leq K,i,j\leq n}(e^{\alpha|(\mathrm{x}_{k})_{ij}|}-1)\leq B, and the constant α\alpha is large. In order to make Pkπ+xkP^{\pi}_{k}+\mathrm{x}_{k} a transition kernel. xk\mathrm{x}_{k} also need to satisfy that ∑j(xk)i​j=0,∀i,k\sum_{j}(\mathrm{x}_{k})_{ij}=0,\forall i,k. By reorganizing these constraints, we get a convex optimization problem with a linear objective function (7).

maxxk⁡maxπk\displaystyle\max_{\mathrm{x}_{k}}\max_{\pi_{k}}\; ∑k=0K⟨Ak,xk⟩,\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{K}\langle A_{k},\mathrm{x}_{k}\rangle, (7)
s.t.  ∑k,i,j(eα​|(xk)i​j|−1)≤B,\displaystyle\sum_{k,i,j}\big(e^{\alpha|(\mathrm{x}_{k})_{ij}|}-1\big)\leq B,
∑j=1n(xk)i​j=0,∀i,k.\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{n}(\mathrm{x}_{k})_{ij}=0,\quad\forall i,k.

Here, the optimization variables are the configurable variables {xk}k=0K\{\mathrm{x}_{k}\}_{k=0}^{K} and {πk}\{\pi_{k}\} are the set of policies the agent can adopt in episode kk. This problem is solvable using classic convex optimization methods. One may even iteratively solve the original problem by performing localized linearization of the original objective function. Compared with previous works on configurable RL for fixed kernel [11], our novelty for this special case is that we are dealing with time-varying non-stationary RL.

4 Bi-level Model-based Value Iteration

Algorithm: We propose the model-based Bi-level value iteration algorithm 1 to solve the Bi-level configurable MDP model proposed in section 2. With the estimations {P^}P^∈𝒫^\{\hat{P}\}_{\hat{P}\in\hat{\mathcal{P}}} and Q^\hat{Q}, we provide the model-based bi-level value iteration algorithm as follows:

To apply Algorithm 1, we need to first estimate the ground-truth lower-level kernels P∈𝒫P\in\mathcal{P} and the ground-truth upper-level kernel QQ. We assume that the reward function r⁡(s,a),∀(s,a)∈𝒮×𝒜r(s,a),\forall(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A} is known and remains the same across all possible lower-level models.

To estimate each ground-truth lower-level kernel P∈𝒫P\in\mathcal{P}, given a dataset DD of trajectories, D={(s1,a1,r1,s2,…,sT+1)}D=\{(s_{1},a_{1},r_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{T+1})\}, and we convert it into a series of {(s,a,r,s′)}\{(s,a,r,s^{\prime})\} tuples. We break each trajectory into TT tuples: (s1,a1,r1,s2),(s2,a2,r2,s3),…,(sT,aT,rT,sT+1)(s_{1},a_{1},r_{1},s_{2}),(s_{2},a_{2},r_{2},s_{3}),\dots,(s_{T},a_{T},r_{T},s_{T+1}). For every state-action pair (s,a)(s,a), let D(s,a)D_{(s,a)} be the subset of tuples where the first element of the tuple is ss, and the second element of the tuple is aa. Then the elements in D(s,a)D_{(s,a)} can be represented by (r,s′)(r,s^{\prime}) since they share the same state-action pair (s,a)(s,a). Each empirical lower-level kernel P^\hat{P} is estimated by the empirical frequency of state transitions, i.e., ∀(s,a)∈𝒮×𝒜,P^​(s′|s,a)=C​o​u​n​t​((r,s′))/|D(s,a)|.\forall(s,a)\in\mathcal{S\times\mathcal{A}},\ \ \hat{P}(s^{\prime}|s,a)=Count((r,s^{\prime}))/\Big|D_{(s,a)}\Big|.

Similarly, to estimate the ground-truth upper-level kernel QQ, given a dataset DqD^{q} of trajectories, Dq={(P1,b1,R1,P2,…,PK+1)}D^{q}=\{(P_{1},b_{1},R_{1},P_{2},\dots,P_{K+1})\}, and we convert it into a series of {(P,b,R,P′)}\{(P,b,R,P^{\prime})\} tuples. We break each trajectory into KK tuples: (P1,b1,R1,P2),(P2,b2,R2,P3),…,(PK,bK,RK,PK+1)(P_{1},b_{1},R_{1},P_{2}),(P_{2},b_{2},R_{2},P_{3}),\dots,(P_{K},b_{K},R_{K},P_{K+1}). For every lower-level kernel (upper-level state) and model-changing-action pair (P,b)(P,b), let D(P,b)qD^{q}_{(P,b)} be the subset of tuples where the first element of the tuple is PP, and the second element of the tuple is bb. Then the elements in D(P,b)qD^{q}_{(P,b)} can be represented by (R,P′)(R,P^{\prime}). The empirical upper-level kernel Q^\hat{Q} is estimated by the empirical frequency of kernel transitions, i.e., ∀(P,b)∈𝒫×ℬ,Q^​(P′|P,b)=C​o​u​n​t​((R,P′))/|D(P,b)q|.\forall(P,b)\in\mathcal{P}\times\mathcal{B},\ \ \hat{Q}(P^{\prime}|P,b)=Count((R,P^{\prime}))/\Big|D^{q}_{(P,b)}\Big|.

Algorithm 1 produces the higher-order state-values WHUW^{H_{U}} and the higher-order policy ΘHU\Theta^{H_{U}}. The higher-order state-value represents the maximum achievable expected returns when the agent jointly optimizes both the environment configuration and its adaptation to the configured environment. The policy ΘHU\Theta^{H_{U}} specifies the optimal model-changing action, i.e., configuration, to apply to the current lower-level kernel. Each lower-level expected return JJ, which is the “average” of lower-level state-values, contributes to the upper-level reward function RR (based on equation (3)). The upper-level MDP makes decisions on model changing according to the information reported by the lower-level MDP. 11 1 We remark that for Algorithm 1, we assume that there are mm possible states for the upper-level MDP, namely there are mm possible transition kernels for the lower-level MDP. Due to configuration error or estimation error, the estimation P^\hat{P} may not be exactly the same as one of the mm possible kernels; however, we assume that those errors are small such that we still regard P^\hat{P} as “in” the set of mm candidate ideal transition kernels and know which set member P^\hat{P} is closest to or associated with.

In the following section, we discuss how the physical limitation of the bi-level MDP model and the estimation error of the model-based algorithm would affect the performance of Algorithm 1. Here the physical limitation error comes from the precision limit of configuration, and the estimation error refers to error of lower-level MDP estimating its configured kernel.

5 Performance analysis

Notations: We define some extra notations for the following analyses: By executing the lower-level policy π:𝒮→𝒜\pi:\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\mathcal{A}, and executing the higher-order policy Θ:𝒫→ℬ\Theta:\mathcal{P}\rightarrow\mathcal{B}:

  • •

    VPcπV_{P_{c}}^{\pi}: the ideal lower-level state-value of the ideally configured lower-level MDP with the ideal transition kernel PcP_{c};

  • •

    VPπV_{P}^{\pi}: the ground-truth lower-level state-value of lower-level ground-truth kernel PP (PP may be different from PcP_{c} due to configuration error);

  • •

    VP^πV_{\hat{P}}^{\pi}: the empirical lower-level state-value of lower-level MDP with empirical transition kernel P^\hat{P};

  • •

    WQΘW^{\Theta}_{Q}: the ideal higher-order state-value of the upper-level MDP with ground-truth kernel QQ, where we also assume the lower-level MDP has the ideal transition kernel PcP_{c};

  • •

    WQ^ΘW^{\Theta}_{\hat{Q}}: the empirical higher-order state-value of the empirical upper-level MDP.

We now present the following estimation error lemma which characterizes the effect of estimation error, highlighting the performance gap which arises from the difference between the true transition kernel PP and its estimation P^\hat{P}.
